blocks.c: She would not let me speak until I had read it.

The lease is not a scroll and it is not written in blood. It is a photocopy. It is eleven pages of dense typed clauses on A4, produced by a machine somewhere off to the left, and Wen had a copy on the desk with thirty-one years of annotations in the margins in four colours of biro.
Clause fourteen is one sentence long.
Where the Caretaker disputes an item in writing, the item shall be held in inventory pending determination, and shall not be applied against the Caretaker's account until the dispute is determined.
"Pending determination," Wen said. "That's the whole gap. You dispute it, it goes in a box, and it sits in a box until somebody determines the dispute. Do you know who determines the dispute?"

"It does. And it has never once, in a hundred and fifty-one years, actually determined one, because determining requires a hearing, and a hearing requires two parties present and signing, and there has never been a second party who could sign." She turned the page round. "Every box out there with a name on it is a dispute nobody filed. Marcus never filed. I filed for four years and then it moved me somewhere I couldn't reach a book."

"The boxes are held, Ravi. Not consumed. Held." Wen's hands were flat on the table and I saw for the first time that they were shaking. "Everything anybody ever lost in this building is forty feet from where you're standing, in cardboard, because I made it file the paperwork and then I made sure nobody was ever able to attend the hearing."
I looked out at the shelving going off into the dark. Hundreds of racks. Thousands of boxes.
"How long have you been running out the clock?"
"Thirty-one years," said Wen Aguilar. "And it renews at dawn."
